gaps.sentence: We see our grandparents ___ other weekend.
gaps.explanation: 'Every other weekend' means alternate weekends; 'each other' has a different, reciprocal meaning.

gaps.sentence: ___ money was spent on advertising last year.
___ lakes in this region freeze in winter.
gaps.explanation: 'Most lakes' speaks about lakes in general; 'most of' would need 'the lakes'.

gaps.sentence: I don't like ___ of these two paintings.
gaps.explanation: After 'don't like', 'either' is used: 'not ... either of them' means zero of the two; 'neither' would double the negative.

gaps.sentence: I'd love ___ help with the decorating, if you're free.
gaps.explanation: 'Some' is used in requests and hopes where the speaker wants agreement.

gaps.sentence: ___ the students passed with good grades.
gaps.explanation: Before 'the + noun' use 'most of': 'Most of the students'; 'most the students' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: There weren't ___ chairs, so some guests had to stand.
gaps.explanation: 'Chairs' is countable and plural, so 'many' fits; 'much' and 'little' are for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: She made very ___ mistakes in the essay, so she nearly got full marks.
gaps.explanation: 'Very few mistakes' means almost none, which explains the high mark; 'mistakes' is countable.
